scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
Good news travels fast: Neo's board signed off on the fielding budget — **600 completes**. Not the 997 you estimated, but close enough to keep the margin of error respectable, and Dana negotiated hard for it.

Before anyone sends a single invitation, we have to answer the question that decides whether those 600 completes are worth anything: **how do we select who gets surveyed?** A sample is only as good as the process that produced it. Pick people the wrong way and it doesn't matter how carefully you wrote the questionnaire — the numbers won't project to Neo's 300,000-household target population.

Two assignments today. First, a diagnostic: I'll show you seven fielding plans that vendors and colleagues have floated for the Neo project, and you'll identify which **sampling technique** each one actually is. Vendors never use the textbook names — they describe a process and let you assume it's rigorous. You have to recognize the technique from the description.

Second, the real decision: from those same seven plans, recommend the **three** that are defensible for Neo's objective. Dana's standard is simple — Neo wants results that describe the target population as a whole, so the plan has to support that claim.

The **Guides** have a field guide to all eight techniques and a short piece on why probability sampling is the price of projectability. Read them first — the seven scenarios are written the way vendors actually talk.

inbox.subject: Board approved fielding — sampling plan due
inbox.body:
Update from this morning's call: **Neo approved a fielding budget for 600 completes.** The board looked at your three sample-size estimates and landed near your first one — they couldn't fund the full n = 997 at 95%/±3.1%, but 600 keeps the margin of error in a range their CFO can present with a straight face. That's a budget compromise I can live with.

What I can't live with is fielding those 600 the wrong way. The sample-size math assumed the sample would be drawn properly — the formula is only honest if the selection process gives it a right to be. So before we brief the panel vendor, I need a **sampling plan recommendation** from our team: which selection methods are defensible for Neo, and which are not.

Marcus has pulled together seven fielding approaches that have been floated for this project — some from vendors, some from well-meaning people at Neo. Work through his exercise first (identify what each approach actually is), then recommend the three plans we could defend in front of Neo's board.

Remember what Neo is buying: numbers that describe **Southern California owner-occupied homeowners meeting the screen — all 300,000 of them** — not just the people who happened to be easy to reach. Keep that sentence in front of you while you work.

Sampling plan is due end of week. Fielding starts the Monday after.

— Dana

inbox.subject: Fair warning: the technique quiz
inbox.body:
Before you touch the recommendation, I'm putting you through the same exercise every analyst here survives: seven sampling scenarios, no labels, you name the technique.

Fair warning — this quiz has teeth. Every scenario is dressed in project language, because that's how it arrives in real life. No vendor ever says "we propose a convenience sample." They say "we'll intercept qualified homeowners at a high-traffic event." Same thing, better outfit.

The two pairs that trip people up, every single time:

1. **Quota vs. stratified.** Both involve subgroups and target counts, and the deliverables look identical on paper. The difference is *how people get into the cells*. Stratified sampling draws **randomly within each subgroup** from a list of the population. Quota sampling fills the same-looking cells with **whoever shows up** until each cell is full. One is probability sampling; the other just wears its costume. Prove you can tell quota from stratified — most people can't.
2. **Systematic vs. simple random.** Both start from a full list and both are probability methods. Simple random draws every record independently by random numbers. Systematic takes a random starting point, then every *k*-th record. If the description has a fixed skip interval, it's systematic — no matter how many times the word "random" appears around it.

Read each scenario for the **selection mechanism**, not the vocabulary. Who is on the list? Who has a chance of being chosen? Is that chance knowable? Answer those three and the technique names itself.

— Marcus

pages.title: Identify the Sampling Technique
pages.intro: Seven fielding plans have been floated for the Neo Smart Living survey. For each scenario, identify the **sampling technique** it describes. Every scenario uses the same eight answer choices — read for the selection *mechanism*, not the marketing language.

pages.title: Recommend Neo's Sampling Plans
pages.intro: Now the recommendation Dana needs. From the same seven fielding plans, select the **three** you would defend in front of Neo's board. The Probability-or-non-probability column is intentionally blank — making that call is your job.

tasks.title: Sampling Technique Identification
tasks.prompt: For each of the seven fielding scenarios below, select the sampling technique being described.

groups.label: Scenario 1 — The expo booth
groups.context: A vendor proposes fielding the entire study at the **SoCal Home & Garden Expo** in Anaheim next month. Two staffers would work Neo's booth, and any attendee who stops by, passes the homeowner screen, and agrees to take the survey on a tablet gets a $5 coffee card — first come, first served, until 600 completes are in. The vendor's pitch: the expo draws exactly the home-improvement-minded homeowners Neo wants, fielding wraps in one weekend, and the incremental cost is close to zero.

groups.label: Scenario 2 — Every 80th record
groups.context: A list broker has sold us a database of **48,000 Southern California homeowners** who pass Neo's screen (owner-occupied single-family, usable yard, income $75K+). The fielding plan: sort the list by ZIP code and street address, pick a random starting point between record 1 and record 80, and then invite **every 80th record** after that — 48,000 ÷ 80 = 600 invitations, working down the sorted list at a fixed skip until the list is exhausted.

groups.label: Scenario 3 — The specialists' picks
groups.context: A panel provider offers its premium tier: a team of in-house **"housing-category specialists"** who personally review panelist profiles and hand-pick the respondents they judge most thoughtful and articulate about home-improvement projects. "We don't leave your sample to chance," their deck says. "Our experts curate 600 respondents who will give Neo rich, considered answers instead of straight-lining through the questionnaire." Selection is entirely at the specialists' discretion, based on their professional read of who belongs in the study.

groups.label: Scenario 4 — Fill the cells
groups.context:
An online-panel vendor proposes opening the survey to its opt-in SoCal panel and letting qualified volunteers pour in — but with hard caps so the final 600 matches target counts by county group and income bracket. Each cell closes the moment it fills, first come, first served:

| County group | $75K–$100K | $100K+ |
|---|---|---|
| Los Angeles & Orange | 150 | 150 |
| San Diego & Inland Empire | 150 | 150 |

No list of the 300,000 households is used; whoever arrives first fills each cell until all four hit 150.

groups.label: Scenario 5 — Refer your neighbors
groups.context: Someone on Neo's marketing team suggests growing the sample through referrals: start with the few dozen homeowners already on Neo's mailing list, and at the end of the questionnaire ask each completing respondent to **refer two or three neighbors who have backyards**. Each referral gets an invitation, completes the survey, and is asked for referrals in turn — the sample recruits itself, chain by chain, wave after wave, until the study reaches 600 completes.

groups.label: Scenario 6 — The random-number draw
groups.context: Using the **SoCal Housing & Lot-Use Atlas**, we can assemble the full frame: all **300,000** Southern California owner-occupied single-family households that meet Neo's yard and income screen, each with a unique record number. The fielding plan: a random-number generator draws record numbers one at a time, each draw independent of every other, and every household on the list has **exactly the same chance** of being selected. Draws continue until 600 households complete the survey.

groups.label: Scenario 7 — Divide, then draw
groups.context:
Same 300,000-household list as Scenario 6, but first the list is **divided into county strata** sized in proportion to each county group's share of the qualified population. Then, **within each stratum**, households are drawn at random until that stratum's allocation completes:

| County stratum | Qualified households | Share | Completes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Los Angeles | 120,000 | 40% | 240 |
| Orange | 60,000 | 20% | 120 |
| San Diego | 54,000 | 18% | 108 |
| Inland Empire | 51,000 | 17% | 102 |
| Ventura | 15,000 | 5% | 30 |

Every household still has a knowable, random chance of selection — the division just guarantees each county lands at its population share of the 600.

guides.title: Sampling techniques field guide
guides.body:
A **sample** stands in for a population. The technique — the rule that decides who gets in — determines whether the sample can speak for the population or only for itself.

The fundamental split is **probability vs. non-probability**. In a probability sample, every member of the population has a *known, nonzero chance* of selection, which requires a **sampling frame** — a list (or map) of the population to draw from. In a non-probability sample, selection depends on convenience, judgment, volunteering, or referral, and no one can say what chance any given person had.

| Technique | How selection works | Probability? | Classic use | Classic failure |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Simple random sampling | Every member of the frame drawn independently by random numbers; equal chance for all | Yes | Gold standard when a full list exists | Impossible without a complete frame; can be costly to reach scattered selections |
| Systematic sampling | Random start, then every k-th record on an ordered list | Yes | Fast, auditable draws from big lists and databases | A hidden repeating pattern in the list that matches the skip interval biases the draw |
| Stratified sampling | Divide the frame into subgroups (strata), then draw randomly within each | Yes | Guaranteeing key subgroups land at their population share; tighter precision | Mistaking it for quota sampling — the within-stratum draw must be random |
| Cluster sampling | Randomly select whole groups (cities, blocks, stores), then survey within the chosen clusters | Yes | Cutting cost when the population is geographically scattered | Clusters that are internally alike understate population variety |
| Convenience sampling | Take whoever is easiest to reach — a location, a class, a website pop-up | No | Quick pilots, pretests, directional reads | Presenting the easy-to-reach as if they were the population |
| Quota sampling | Set target counts per cell, fill each cell with whoever comes until it's full | No | Making a non-random sample's demographics resemble the population | Matched demographics hide non-random selection inside every cell |
| Snowball sampling | Start with a few members, ask each for referrals, repeat | No | Rare or hard-to-list populations (specialists, niche communities) | Chains stay inside one social network; the sample inherits its connections |
| Judgment (expert) sampling | An expert hand-picks the members they believe belong in the study | No | Selecting a handful of information-rich cases for qualitative work | The sample reflects the expert's beliefs — the very thing the study was meant to test |

**Reading a fielding plan.** Vendors describe processes, not textbook labels. Ask three questions of any plan: (1) Is there a *list of the population* behind the draw? (2) Does *chance* — not availability, referral, or human judgment — decide who gets in? (3) Could you compute each person's probability of selection? Three yeses = probability sampling. Any no = non-probability, whatever the plan calls itself.

**The two costume parties.** Quota sampling dresses up as stratified — both have subgroup targets, but only stratified draws randomly *within* the subgroups from a frame. Systematic dresses up as simple random — both are probability methods off a list, but systematic uses a fixed skip interval after a random start, while simple random makes every draw independently.

guides.title: The projectability test
guides.body:
**The claim a survey makes.** When a report says "41% of Southern California homeowners would consider a backyard unit," it is claiming the sample's 41% stands in for the *population's* percentage. That claim — projectability (statisticians say *generalizability*) — is not free. It is purchased with a probability sampling method, and there is no other currency.

**Why probability is the price.** Statistical inference works because random selection makes the sample's errors *predictable in the aggregate*. If every member of the population had a known chance of selection, the mathematics of sampling distributions applies, and we can say how far the sample estimate is likely to sit from the population truth. Remove the randomness and the mathematics has nothing to grip: the sample may be off by a little or a lot, in either direction, and *no one can quantify which*.

**Margin of error is a licensed product.** A margin of error ("±4 percentage points at 95% confidence") is only defensible when it is computed from a probability sample. Attach one to a convenience, quota, snowball, or judgment sample and the number is decoration — the formula's assumptions were never met. This matters here: the sample-size estimates from the last round *assumed* probability selection. Field the same 600 people non-randomly and the precision math they were built on no longer applies.

**What non-probability samples are for.** They are not worthless — they are quick, cheap, and fine for pilots, pretests, idea generation, and hard-to-list populations. Quota sampling in particular is widely used in industry because it *looks* demographically representative. But a quota sample's resemblance to the population is cosmetic: inside every cell, respondents still selected themselves. When the client's decision requires describing the population as a whole — and a board will present the numbers as facts about the market — the fielding plan must be a probability plan.

**The test, in one sentence.** Before recommending any plan, ask: *if the board challenges these numbers, can we defend the claim that every qualified household had a known chance of being heard?*
